passage: Week three of keeping his friend Rukmini's secret, Sunil could recite her moods like a timetable: quiet before tests, crying behind the library shelves on Thursdays, "I'm fine" whenever anyone walked past. She had said that if he told anyone she would never speak to him again, and he believed her. So in the dining hall he laughed with the others, carried her tray when she couldn't, and lay awake in his hostel bed, afraid of what a silent phone might mean. His hands shook over his chapters. Mr Dutta, the hostel warden, stopped by his table. "Everything all right, Sunil? You look worn out." Sunil's mouth opened. "Yes, sir. Just exams." Mr Dutta nodded slowly and said his door stayed open. Across the hall Rukmini's seat was empty again, and nobody who could help knew why.

qa.q: Who asked Sunil if everything was all right?
qa.a: Mr Dutta, the hostel warden, asked Sunil that.

qa.q: What was Sunil afraid of when he kept quiet?
qa.a: Sunil feared that Rukmini would never speak to him again, and he was also afraid of what a silent phone might mean.

qa.q: What different approach could work here, and why?
qa.a: Sunil could go to Mr Dutta, whose door stays open, so trained adults can support Rukmini and Sunil no longer carries it alone.

qa.q: How might Mr Dutta see Sunil's answer?
qa.a: Mr Dutta sees a worn-out student and cannot know why, so he offers his open door, but without more information he cannot help Rukmini.

grounding: A student keeps a friend's distress secret for weeks to protect the friendship, carrying too much and delaying care.

passage:
Dear Shreya Ma'am,
I've been carrying something for five weeks, and I can't any more.
In October my friend Nikhil told me he was hurting himself, and made me swear not to tell. I kept the secret because I thought if I told, he'd never trust me again, and he'd have nobody. So I checked on him every night. I stopped going to football so I'd always be free if he called.
I'm not sleeping. I jump every time my phone buzzes. And Nikhil isn't better. I think he's worse, and all this time the only person who knew was me.
I know now that this is too big for me. Please help him. I'll come to your room at lunch.
Tanvir, 10A

Reply, 11:05 am:
Tanvir, thank you for telling me. You are not in trouble, and you did the right thing. I have called Nikhil in now and I am contacting his parents this morning. Come at lunch; we'll talk about how you are, too.
Shreya Ma'am

qa.q: How long had Tanvir kept the secret?
What made Tanvir keep the secret for so long?
qa.a: Tanvir was afraid of losing Nikhil's trust and worried that telling would leave Nikhil with nobody.

qa.q: What would have helped more back in October?
qa.a: Telling Shreya Ma'am or a parent straight away, so Nikhil got real care weeks sooner and Tanvir wasn't carrying it alone.

qa.q: How might Shreya Ma'am see Tanvir's letter?
qa.a: Shreya Ma'am sees a frightened student who finally reached out, and acts at once for Nikhil while also caring for Tanvir.

grounding: Shows a student keeping a friend's distress secret for weeks to protect the friendship, carrying too heavy a burden and delaying real care.

subtype: Approach: keeping the secret to protect the friendship [Pitfall]
passage:
Ganga Didi, you once asked me why I went so quiet in Class Nine. I'm Mridul, and I think I can finally say it.
My friend Rohit had told me things were really bad at home, and that sometimes he wished he could just disappear. He made me promise. And I thought a real friend keeps promises. If I told, I'd lose him.
So for six weeks I carried it. I watched him in class. I lay awake wondering whether he was okay. I couldn't concentrate on anything; I was fourteen and trying to be his only safety net. And the whole time, nobody who could actually help him even knew.
It ended on a Thursday, when he didn't come to school. I panicked and told our class teacher before first period. She phoned his mother at once, found out he was at home and safe, and by evening the counsellor and his parents were involved.
He's okay now. But those six weeks, Didi, were six weeks he could have had help.

qa.q: How long did Mridul carry the secret?
Why did Mridul keep the promise at first?
qa.a: Mridul was afraid of losing Rohit, believing a real friend keeps promises, and felt it was the loyal thing to do.

qa.q: What could Mridul have done on the day Rohit first told him?
qa.a: Tell the class teacher or a parent that same day, so adults could reach Rohit's family and arrange help at once.

qa.q: What were those six weeks like for Rohit?
qa.a: Rohit was struggling at home with no adult aware, so he went without help that could have started much sooner.

grounding: Shows a student keeping a friend's distress secret for weeks to protect the friendship, carrying a burden too heavy for a teenager and delaying real care.
